title: Building partnerships with local industry and TVET institutions
description: A practical guide for Kenyan senior school principals on building genuine partnerships with local businesses and TVET institutions that create real opportunities for students.
body:
CBE's design explicitly anticipates stronger links between schools and the world of work — through pathway specialisation and an emphasis on practical competency. Yet many Kenyan senior schools have not built meaningful relationships with local employers or TVET institutions, missing an opportunity to give students genuine exposure and pathways that a classroom alone cannot provide.

Why these partnerships matter under CBE

Students in the STEM, Social Sciences, and Arts and Sports Science pathways benefit enormously from seeing how their subjects connect to real careers and industries in their region. A partnership with a local business, hospital, agricultural enterprise, or TVET institution turns abstract subject content into visible, concrete relevance — which both motivates students and informs their career decision-making.

Starting with what already exists locally

Most schools do not need to look far to find potential partners — local businesses, county government offices, health facilities, agricultural cooperatives, and TVET institutions in the area are often open to engagement if approached with a clear, specific proposal rather than a vague request for "partnership."

What a partnership can practically offer

  • Guest speakers who bring real-world context to classroom subjects
  • Site visits that give students direct exposure to work environments related to their pathway
  • Short-term attachment or shadowing opportunities for Grade 11 and 12 students
  • Career guidance input from professionals who can speak credibly about specific fields
  • In some cases, resource or equipment support that benefits practical subject delivery

Practical starting point: Identify three to five local organisations relevant to your school's pathway offerings and approach them with a specific, modest proposal — a single guest talk, or one site visit for a specific class — rather than an open-ended partnership request. A successful small engagement is the foundation for a longer relationship.

TVET institutions as genuine partners, not fallback referrals

Building a direct relationship with a nearby TVET institution — inviting them to present to students, arranging visits, understanding their specific programme offerings — allows your school's career guidance to present TVET pathways with real, current information rather than generic or outdated impressions. This benefits students genuinely suited to a TVET pathway who might otherwise default to university applications due to social pressure alone.

Formalising the relationship over time

What begins as a single guest talk or visit can, over successive years, develop into a more structured relationship — an annual career day, a standing attachment programme, or a resource-sharing arrangement. These relationships develop through consistent follow-through and genuine value on both sides, not through a single ambitious proposal that is never sustained.

Documenting and communicating the value

Sharing the outcomes of these partnerships with parents and the wider school community — a student's positive attachment experience, a successful TVET placement, a well-received guest speaker session — reinforces the value of the initiative and can attract further partnership interest from other organisations who see the school's genuine engagement with its community.
